(Today through Wednesday)...
Issued at 116 AM EDT Thu Aug 13 2026

Overview.

Warm and humid weather continues today across central Indiana with 
additional showers and thunderstorms. Heavy rainfall will lead to a 
continued threat for flash flooding, particularly across north 
central Indiana towards the overnight where slow moving storms are 
likely to bring additional very heavy rain. A few storms could also 
produce strong to damaging wind gusts during the afternoon and 
evening hours. Rain chances persist into Friday and Saturday as a 
frontal system moves through the region. Temperatures will briefly 
warm into the upper 80s and lower 90s on Saturday and Sunday before 
a cold front pushes through. Behind this front, high pressure will 
bring a stretch of drier, less humid, and pleasant weather from 
Monday through Wednesday.

Thursday and Friday.

Central Indiana remains positioned along the northeastern 
periphery of a broad upper-level ridge centered over the South-
Central US, maintaining NW flow aloft with embedded shortwaves 
traversing the region. At the surface, a quasi-stationary 
convective outflow boundary rests across southern Central Indiana.
Latest ACARs soundings show an unseasonably moist atmospheric 
profile with PWAT values ranging from 2.00 to 2.25 inches, 
exceeding the 90th percentile for mid-August. High moisture 
convergence along the boundary combined with deep warm-cloud layer
depths greater than 4000 meters will drive high precipitation 
efficiency and warm rain processes. HREF probability-matched mean 
guidance highlights isolated 2 to 4 inch QPF amounts where cell 
training occurs. Given antecedent low FFG values from recent 
convective rounds, a Flood Watch remains in effect across most of 
central Indiana

Thermodynamically, diurnal heating will yield SBCAPE values of 1500 
to 2500 J/kg, though poor mid-level lapse rates of 5.5 to 6.0 C/km 
will limit the higher end threat for severe weather. However, 
effective bulk shear of 30 to 35 kts coupled with DCAPE values near 
800 to 1000 J/kg will support organized cell clusters and short 
bowing segments. Damaging straight-line winds driven by convective 
downdrafts remain the primary severe threat through Thursday 
evening. The main threat looks to be during the late evening and 
early overnight hours when another quasi-stationary complex of 
showers and storms looks to impact central Indiana with the 
potential additional flash flooding. The exact location of this axis 
remains uncertain, but confidence is highest in a northwest to 
southeast band from approximately along to slightly north of the I-
74 corridor. Broadly, much of central Indiana is likely to see 1-2.5 
inches but within this axis there will be the potential for pockets 
of 3-6 inches.

On Friday, another subtle shortwave moving through the Upper Midwest 
will induce low-level warm air advection and a strengthening LLJ of 
25-35kts. The surface front that has helped to drive rain chances 
will become subtle enough to no longer be a factor in precipitation 
with any showers and storms instead being driven by the shortwave 
aloft. Overall, chances are fairly low outside of any residual 
boundaries from Thursdays convection.

Saturday through Wednesday.

Models have been trending to a weaker ridge over the Central Plains 
which will keep the pattern active over the Ohio Valley as the jet 
stream won't be shunted to the north further into the Great Lakes. 
Southwesterly boundary-layer advection will help push surface 
temperatures into the upper 80s and lower 90s. High dewpoints in the 
mid-70s will yield heat indices approaching 100 degrees across 
southern counties. A northern stream upper-level trough over Canada 
will sweep a surface cold front across the Great Lakes and Ohio 
Valley Sunday into Monday. Convective initiation is expected along 
the front as MLCAPE reaches 1500 to 2000 J/kg amid 30 to 40 kts of 0-
6 km bulk shear. Multicell lines capable of strong wind gusts and 
brief heavy rain will accompany the cold frontal passage.

As the surface cold front exits to the south, allowing a ~1020 mb 
surface high pressure system to build southward from the Canadian 
Prairies into the Great Lakes. Advection of air from the northwest 
will help to bring drier and slightly cooler air into the area late 
Monday through Wednesday with broadly quiet weather.
